title: Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts
text:
Almost a million young people – one in eight – in the UK are not in education, employment or training (Neet).
Having reached the highest level in a decade, the government is seeking to bring that number down after the recommendations made in Alan Milburn’s landmark report.
However, the Neet population is not uniform – making Britain’s youth jobs crisis tougher to respond to. Here we outline the diverse backgrounds of the group struggling to make the transition from school to the world of work on a sustainable basis.
The highest level in a decade
An estimated 981,000 of 16- to 24-year-olds in the UK are Neet, accounting for 13% of that age group, according to official figures – close to the highest level since 2014.
Experts say there are myriad reasons for the high numbers, including the legacies of austerity and the Covid pandemic, rising mental ill health, fewer entry-level jobs, rising costs and taxes for businesses, AI disrupting the jobs market, and employers cutting recruitment as the Middle East war damages Britain’s economy.
Unemployment among the under-25s has risen at the fastest rate since the 2008 financial crisis. Young people now make up about 40% of all unemployment.
This has compounded by a drop in entry-level jobs: over the last 20 years the number of mid- and lower-skilled positions has fallen by about 1.6m. Higher-skilled jobs have risen by about 6.3m. The Saturday job has declined, and automation and AI are replacing entry-level roles.
Falling behind other countries
The UK has a much higher youth unemployment gap – the rate relative to the rest of the working-age population – than any other G7 country. Job opportunities have deteriorated more and Neet rates have risen.
Britain’s headline Neet rate is above average among wealthy countries and has been falling behind. A decade ago the UK was close to the EU average. By 2025, only Romania had a higher rate.
The Netherlands is the European gold standard, with a rate of about 5%. Experts say this is down to higher rates of vocational education and prioritisation of work experience in schools. In contrast, work experience participation is below average and overqualification is high in the UK by international standards.
Stark regional divisions
The Neet challenge is uneven across the UK – reflecting a lack of job opportunities in places with weaker local economies.
Analysis for Milburn’s interim report shows eight of the 10 English local authorities with the highest likelihood of being Neet are in the north of England and the Midlands. In Blackpool, almost a quarter of young people are Neet. In Bath, the rate is fewer than one in 10.
The Youth Futures Foundation shows the risk of a young person becoming Neet is highest in Blackpool, Birmingham, and Bradford. A report by the IPPR thinktank showed there was also a sixfold gap in job opportunities for young people in Rotherham relative to the Cotswolds.
Health
Rising ill health has plagued Britain at large – with long-term sickness among all working-age adults close to a record high. For young people the picture is particularly stark.
Almost half of Neets report having a disability, compared with a fifth of the overall youth population. The rates for both have doubled in the past decade.
Experts say the rise in ill health among young people since 2015 has been primarily driven by issues with mental health. This is partly explained by improved identification and diagnosis. But wider social and economic factors play a role – including the rise of social media and smartphones. After the turmoil of the Covid pandemic – hitting the critical final years of education for young people – a deterioration that was already under way was accelerated.
Figures show a fifth of Neets report issues with depression, mental health and nervous disorders – a sharp rise from just 8% in 2012. The rates for learning difficulties and autism have also tripled. Those with special educational needs or disabilities are about 80% more likely to be Neet.
The risk of Neet indicators
Despite the focus on welfare in Milburn’s report, almost half of Neets (46%) do not claim benefits.
Young women were historically more likely to be Neet. But growing difficulties for young men – with health, the erosion of traditional employment routes, and worsening educational outcomes – alongside a sharp drop in teenage pregnancy rates flipped things in the late 2010s.
In terms of ethnicity, those from Black, African and Caribbean backgrounds have the highest Neet rate, at just over 15%. Those from Chinese backgrounds have the lowest rate, at just under 9%. The rates are connected significantly with wider socioeconomic factors, highlighting the intersectional nature of Britain’s youth jobs crisis.
Young people from disadvantaged backgrounds are at most risk. Those from lower-working class households are more than twice as likely to be Neet than those from higher professional ones.
Experts say the biggest “risk of Neet” indicators include low academic qualifications, having a limiting disability or caring for children. Having parents without qualifications or who are unemployed, being from a single-parent background, growing up in care, periods of school absence or exclusion, and having police or social services contact are also risk factors.
Among young people who are currently Neet, almost a third (29%) finished their education at GCSE level. About a fifth have no qualifications. Those with higher or degree-level qualifications account for about 18%.
While non-graduates face a tougher outlook, graduate hiring in the UK has fallen recently – pushing up their chances of becoming Neet, and adding further to the competition for entry-level jobs.
